Second State Now Investigating Ex-Cardinals Exec Ryan Gold

Published August 23, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Massachusetts Gaming Commission has opened its own inquiry into Ryan Gold, the Arizona Cardinals' former director of college scouting, examining unusual betting patterns tied to him in the state. It's the second state gaming regulator to investigate Gold, following an inquiry the Arizona Department of Gaming opened in July, and it comes after the NFL itself handed Gold an indefinite suspension over separate findings.

What the NFL says happened

Gold, who spent 13 years with the Cardinals organization before rising to director of college scouting, was suspended indefinitely by the NFL in July. The league's findings, as reported, center on two things: that Gold disclosed confidential draft information before it was publicly announced, and that he participated in football wagering himself, including parlays involving NFL and college games — both violations of the NFL's personnel gambling policy, which bars employees from betting on football, assisting others with bets, or sharing non-public information that could be used for betting purposes. Gold has an appeal hearing scheduled for September 23. His attorney, Mike Caspino, has denied the allegations, calling the league's investigation "deeply flawed."

Why two states are now involved

State gaming regulators run their own integrity monitoring independent of league discipline, watching for unusual betting patterns that could indicate insider information was used to place wagers. Arizona's inquiry, opened in July, looks at betting activity connected to Gold within that state. Massachusetts' newer investigation is examining separate unusual betting patterns tied to Gold there — notable partly because Gold is a Massachusetts native and University of Massachusetts graduate, giving regulators there a direct local angle to examine. Neither state has announced findings or concluded its review.

Why it matters to bettors

Cases like this are part of why leagues and states have leaned harder into integrity monitoring as legal sports betting has expanded — a team employee's non-public knowledge, if actually used for betting or shared with someone who bets on it, is exactly the kind of information asymmetry that legal, regulated markets are built to guard against. For everyday bettors, stories like this are a reminder that unusual line or handle movement on a specific market can trigger real regulatory scrutiny, and that the leagues themselves increasingly treat insider-information gambling violations as seriously as, or more seriously than, other conduct issues. The case remains open on both the NFL appeal and the state regulatory side, so nothing here is resolved yet.
